Colophon

How this is built.

Four experiments in methods that usually mean importing a library. Each one is raw platform code — and each one still works with a keyboard, still respects reduced motion, and still says something useful when the effect is switched off.

The rules

No dependencies, still

The whole portfolio ships zero runtime dependencies, and the lab does not get an exemption for being the hard part. A renderer you imported proves you can read documentation; one you wrote proves something else.

Motion is optional, always

Every experiment checks prefers-reduced-motion and has a considered static state — not a blank box. Continuous animation carries a pause control, because WCAG 2.2.2 is not waived for being pretty.

Canvas is invisible to assistive technology

A canvas element is a bitmap with no semantics. Everything drawn in one here is also available as text, a table or a control — so the experiments are described rather than merely decorated.

The scrollbar is not yours to take

No smooth-scroll hijack, no wheel interception, no scroll-jacking. The page scrolls the way the operating system says it scrolls, and the visualisation reads that position.

What was not shipped

Not an argument that these libraries are bad — they are excellent, and on a project with a deadline most of them are the right call. The point is that writing the thing yourself is the only way to find out whether you could.

Libraries the experiments would normally have needed
Library Typical weight Replaced in
three.js ~600 KB Renderer
matter.js ~90 KB Verlet
GSAP + ScrollTrigger ~120 KB Descent
A smooth-scroll library ~25 KB Descent

The stack, such as it is

Static HTML generated by a dependency-free Node script. Plain CSS with custom properties. ES modules served directly to the browser — no bundler, no transpiler, no build step beyond writing files out.

The whole portfolio, all five sites, is under two megabytes. The lab's four experiments add roughly 30 KB of JavaScript between them, which is less than the smallest library any one of them replaces.

Every page is checked before it ships: broken links, metadata, heading structure, structured data, form labelling and unlabelled graphics all fail the build. The experiments are additionally driven end to end in a real browser.

Where the seams are

The renderer has no shadow mapping, no post-processing and no scene graph. It renders one object well. An engine gives you all three on day one, and for anything with more than a handful of objects that is the correct trade.

The physics is 2D and position-based. No rigid bodies, no rotation, no continuous collision detection. It is the right tool for cloth and rope and the wrong one for a stack of crates.

Two of the four experiments need JavaScript to show anything. The renderer and the physics degrade to an explanation rather than a demo. Descent and Motion both work without it.

Naming these is the point of a colophon. Work that only lists what it does well is advertising.

Meridian Lab is in-house research by Studio Meridian. The client work is on the studio site.
